extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political history, criminology, and policing studies
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the political, legal, media, and social indicators that mark the shift toward a 'law-and-order' or 'exceptional' state in Britain around 1970–1972. Use features in rhetoric, legislation, policing, courts, media and labour relations as diagnostic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift to control / escalation to state level
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There begins the regular, immediate escalation of every conflictual issue up the hierarchy of control to the level of the state machine - each issue is instantly appropriated by the apparatuses of politics, government, the courts, the police or the law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an indicator when local conflicts are routinely reframed and handled by central state institutions (ministers, courts, national police) rather than local or informal resolution; the text contrasts a pre-June upward spiral of local pressure with a post-1970 automatic pincer thrust of popular moral pressure from below and control from above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routinisation of repression
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The decisive mechanisms in the management of hegemonic control in the period after June 1970 are regularly and routinely based in the apparatuses of constraint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for normalization of repressive measures — legal, police and administrative — becoming routine instruments of governance rather than exceptional responses; the campaign 'toned up and groomed the society for the extensive exercise of the repressive side of state power.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimation of recourse to law and statutory power
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The law-and-order campaign ... had the overwhelming single consequence of legitimating the recourse to the law, to constraint and statutory power ... It made this routinisation of control normal, natural, and thus right and inevitable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify rhetorical and policy moves that present use of law and coercion as the appropriate, inevitable response to social problems; assess how such legitimation expands the perceived remit of the state to 'go campaigning.'

rubrics_metrics.name: State campaigning and exemplary prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: State agents increasingly 'go campaigning' with 'the full force of the repressive side of the state ... openly and systematically turned against this anarchist disorderly flank' and prosecutions became progressively more serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes targeted arrests, exemplary trials (e.g., Garden House students), and prosecutorial encouragement from police/DPP; criterion flags systematic use of courts to deter protest and dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactivation and legal engineering (use of conspiracy/trespass/riot laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to create new trespass law led to the 'reactivation of the ancient law of conspiracy' and giving new life to charges of 'unlawful and riotous assembly' as instruments against protest and industrial militancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legislative and prosecutorial choices that resurrect or repurpose old common‑law offences (conspiracy, riotous assembly) when newer laws fail, as a marker of legal adaptation to repress movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media amplification and acceptance of government paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: The media 'accepted the government's paradigm 'explanation' for industrial unrest' and helped percolate a conspiratorial reading of Britain's troubles; both hysterical and sober papers lent support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the extent to which mainstream media promulgate or normalize state framings (e.g., identifying 'militants' as drivers of problems), thereby amplifying moral panic and legitimating policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of moral panic and the 'enemy'
rubrics_metrics.description: The law-and-order themes orchestrated together 'constructed nightmares' and raised the 'nemesis of anarchy' to the level of the state; moral panic feeds on discrepancies between perceived danger and remedies proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for rhetorical moves that conflate diverse social phenomena into a single threatening 'enemy' (students, long hair, crime, immigrants), and for moral‑panic dynamics where exaggerated danger legitimates extraordinary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of targets from demonstrators/minorities to the working class
rubrics_metrics.description: Although initially aimed at demonstrators, Black Power activists, squatters and students, the campaign broadened to 'discipline, restrain and coerce' solid ranks of the working class (unions, striking workers) as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as criterion when policing/legislation and prosecutions shift from marginal protest groups to mainstream labour movement targets (Industrial Relations Bill, attacks on picketing, legal sanctions against unions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial endorsement of deterrence (deterrent sentencing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial statements such as 'A DETERRENT sentence is not meant to fit the offender, it is meant to fit the offence' and confirmation of uniform heavy sentences regardless of individual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag judicial pronouncements and sentencing practices that prioritize deterrence over individualized justice as evidence of judicial complicity in a law-and-order regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police harassment and racialised policing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp rise in confrontations between black communities and police, allegations of brutality, drug planting, harassment and targeted raids (e.g., Mangrove), and complaints overwhelming community relations bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sustained patterns of police harassment of minority communities, multiple complaints, and lack of satisfactory police rebuttal as indicators of racially biased, coercive policing within the law-and-order shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative strategy to constrain labour (Industrial Relations Bill etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Industrial Relations Bill and other proposed measures sought a 'tight framework of constraints in the industrial-relations field, backed by the courts and fines; attack on picketting; if necessary, exemplary arrests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence and content of legislation intended to curtail union activity, impose personal liabilities, or otherwise legalize coercion in industrial disputes as markers of state strategy to discipline labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political rhetoric framing unity and stigmatizing outsiders
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservative appeals to 'one nation', 'safeguard the unity of the nation', and stigmatization of those outside the national consensus as 'extremists' provided a 'positive face' to law-and-order themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify political discourse that frames repression as defense of national unity and uses stigmatization to marginalize dissenting groups — a legitimating device for coercive policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental/pragmatic ('English') path to authoritarian measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'English tendency to do softly softly, pragmatically piece-meal what other countries do in one fell, dramatic swoop' — a crab-like, incremental approach to building repressive capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a process criterion: look for piecemeal legal, administrative and policing changes that cumulatively produce significant loss of civil liberties rather than a single sweeping law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling of economic policy with repressive labour discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Heath's economic strategy (freeing market forces, letting 'lame ducks' sink) required disciplining labour by law: rising unemployment, inflation, and explicit legal constraints on labour were seen as mechanisms to hold labour in line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether economic liberalization or austerity policies are deliberately paired with legal and policing measures to control labour — an integrated political-economic criterion for the exceptional state.
